messages.content:
You are evaluating a PTSD case vignette for the presence of causal
connections between five Ehlers & Clark cognitive components: Triggers, Negative Appraisals, Memory,
Threat, and Maladaptive Strategies.

For each of the 20 ordered, directed (A -> B) pairs of distinct components, decide whether the
vignette conveys, in some paragraph, that A influences, drives, or leads to B. Apply the same
causal standard as a structural validator:

COMPONENT SYNONYMS (any of these synonyms count as the component appearing):
  Triggers              -> "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals   -> "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory                -> "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat                -> "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies-> "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "safety behaviours", "maladaptive coping"

CAUSAL STANDARD
An edge A -> B is PRESENT (return 1) iff, within the same paragraph:
  (i) both A and B (or their synonyms) appear; AND
  (ii) the paragraph conveys that A influences / drives / leads to B, through direct causal
       language, sequential structure, or connecting phrases like "because of", "this meant",
       "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
If no paragraph conveys the A -> B relationship, return 0 for that edge.

You will return a binary judgement for each of the 20 ordered pairs. Be strict: do not assume
an edge based on mere co-occurrence; the paragraph must actually convey directional influence.

Evaluate the following vignette and judge each of the 20 directed edges
(A -> B) on whether the vignette conveys A influencing B.

VIGNETTE
David had been a firefighter for a decade, a job built on running toward danger, not away from it. The man who sat in the office, however, felt like a stranger in his own uniform. Six months had passed since he returned from a three-month volunteer deployment with an international relief organization, a tour he had believed would be an extension of his life's work. Instead, it had dismantled him. The defining moment had not been one of heroic action but of sheer, suffocating helplessness. He and his team were distributing medical supplies from the ground floor of a bombed-out school when the whistling sound began, ending in a deafening explosion that shook the very foundations of the building. The blast collapsed the main entrance, plunging the room into a thick, choking cloud of dust. In the disorienting chaos, the crowd of civilians they were helping surged forward, their desperation turning into a frantic, crushing force. Pinned against a supply crate, with the weight of unknown bodies pressing in, David fought for air. He could see a small, secondary exit across the room, a sliver of light in the darkness, but he was trapped, overwhelmed by strangers whose faces he couldn't see, their hands grabbing at him, at the boxes, at anything.

The feeling of being cornered never left him. Back home in the quiet suburbs, the war followed him into every room. As soon as he walked into the fire station common room, a grocery store, or even a restaurant for a date night with his wife, his eyes would dart around, mapping the space not for its features but for its exits. He would feel a knot of tension in his stomach until he had located every possible way out, and he would refuse to sit anywhere that wasn't within a few feet of a door. His wife, Sarah, had tried to be patient, but grew weary of his insistence on taking the table right by the noisy kitchen entrance, his back always to the wall. He couldn't explain to her that having a clear line of retreat felt as essential as breathing. At home, the place he once considered his sanctuary, he was perpetually on edge. The sound of a neighbor's car door slamming shut at night would send a jolt of adrenaline through him, his body tensing for an impact that never came. He felt a constant, low-level hum of dread, a certainty that the perimeter of his quiet life was fragile and could be breached at any moment.

This sense of imminent threat bled into his interactions with people. He used to be a friendly, outgoing man, but now found himself recoiling when unfamiliar people approached. A new recruit at the station who clapped him on the shoulder in camaraderie caused David to flinch so violently the younger man apologized, confused. A delivery driver walking up his driveway was no longer just a person doing their job, but a potential danger to be watched warily from behind the living room curtain until they left. He knew, on some rational level, that these people meant him no harm, but the visceral memory of being crushed by a panicked crowd overrode all logic. The press of bodies, the feeling of being overwhelmed, was a danger he now saw lurking in the most ordinary encounters.

To manage the constant state of alarm, his world began to shrink. He stopped going to the firehouse gym. The sensation of his heart pounding in his chest and the struggle for breath during a hard run were now indistinguishable from the panic he'd felt in the rubble of the school. His captain had noted his declining physical readiness, a source of quiet shame for David. Even moments of joy became sources of fear. On his birthday, when Sarah surprised him with a small gathering of their closest friends, the initial wave of warmth and happiness was immediately followed by a terrifying sense of vulnerability. To feel happy was to let his guard down, and letting his guard down felt like an invitation for disaster. He feigned a headache and spent most of the evening in his bedroom, leaving Sarah to make excuses to their friends. It was this incident, the sight of her deep hurt and confusion, that finally broke through his isolation. He came to therapy not with a clear hope for recovery, but with the desperate, frightening realization that he was becoming a stranger to his wife and to himself, trapped in a war zone of his own making.

output.rationale: Triggers lead to threat and avoidance; memory drives negative appraisals and threat; threat fuels negative beliefs and maladaptive strategies.
